In Brazil devotion to them is very popular and connected with children: in many Catholic families, at the end of September, sweets are handed out in thanksgiving for graces received. Their liturgical feast is celebrated on September 26. They remind us that science and work can be lived as free service to our neighbor.
rita-cassia:
The girl from Roccaporena

Rita was born in 1381 in Roccaporena, near Cascia in Umbria, the only daughter of elderly parents known in the region as peacemakers. From childhood she longed to consecrate herself to God in a convent, but, as was common at the time, her parents gave her in marriage while still young to a man named Paolo, who had a violent temper.

Wife and mother amid violence

For about eighteen years Rita patiently endured her husband's mistreatment, praying for him, until he was converted and began to live in peace. They had two sons. But Paolo, caught up in the feuds between families of the region, was murdered. The sons, now young men, swore to avenge their father. Rita, fearing they would lose their souls by committing murder, asked God to take them before that happened. Soon afterward both fell ill and died, reconciled with God. Alone, Rita worked to make the enemy families make peace and forgave her husband's killers.

The nun of the thorn

She then wanted to enter the Augustinian monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene in Cascia, but was refused three times because she was a widow and because of her family's history of violence. An ancient tradition says that one night she was miraculously carried into the monastery by Saint John the Baptist, Saint Augustine and Saint Nicholas of Tolentino. Once accepted, she lived about forty years in prayer, penance and obedience; it is said that for a long time she watered a dry stick at her superior's command, and it sprouted. In 1442, after hearing a sermon on the Passion, she asked to share in Christ's sufferings and received on her forehead a wound like that of a thorn from the crown, which she bore for fifteen years.

The saint of roses

Already ill, in the depths of winter, she asked a relative for a rose and figs from the garden of her old home; the relative went without hope and found a rose in bloom and ripe figs. Rita died on May 22, 1457, and her body is venerated in Cascia. Canonized in 1900, she is invoked as patron of impossible causes, of wives in difficult marriages and of reconciliation. On her feast, roses are blessed in churches.
isabel-hungria:
A princess betrothed as a child

Elizabeth was born in 1207, the daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary. At four she was promised in marriage to Louis, heir to Thuringia in Germany, and taken to the castle of Wartburg, where she grew up alongside him. At fourteen she married Louis, by then landgrave of Thuringia. It was a marriage of true love: the two prayed together, and Louis supported his wife in her generosity toward the poor. They had three children.

Queen of the poor

Moved by the example of the Franciscan friars who were arriving in Germany, Elizabeth lived simply despite her position. She went down from the castle carrying bread to the hungry, personally cared for the sick and, during a great famine, distributed the grain from the royal granaries. She had a hospital built at the foot of the castle. A much-loved legend tells that once, carrying loaves hidden in her cloak, she was stopped, and when she opened the cloak there were only roses.

A widow at twenty

In 1227 Louis left on a crusade and died of illness in Italy. On receiving the news, Elizabeth cried out that for her the world had died. A widow at twenty, according to tradition she was forced to leave the castle of Wartburg with her small children and suffered want. Later, with her children's future secured, she renounced her possessions, became a Franciscan tertiary and, under the strict guidance of her confessor, Conrad of Marburg, founded a hospital in Marburg where she served the poorest sick and lepers with her own hands.

Saint of charity

Worn out by work and penance, she died on November 17, 1231, only twenty-four years old. She was canonized just four years later. She is the patron of the Franciscan Third Order, of works of charity and of bakers. Her life shows that it is possible to be a saint in any position, even in a palace, when the heart is turned toward God and the poor.
monica:
A patient wife

Monica was born around 331 in Thagaste, in North Africa, into a Christian family. While still young she was given in marriage to Patricius, a pagan man with an explosive temper who was unfaithful to her. She also lived with a difficult mother-in-law. Instead of responding with quarrels, Monica won her family over with patience, kindness and prayer. Little by little she gained her mother-in-law's respect, and shortly before his death Patricius asked for Baptism.

A mother's tears

Monica had three children, among them Augustine, very intelligent and restless. She watched with sorrow as her son abandoned the faith, lived a dissolute life and joined the sect of the Manichaeans. For years she wept and prayed for him. A bishop, tired of her pleading, consoled her by saying: "Go in peace; it is not possible that the son of so many tears should be lost." When Augustine decided to go to Rome, he deceived his mother and sailed without her. Monica did not give up: she followed him to Italy and found him in Milan.

The joy of conversion

In Milan Monica met Bishop Ambrose, who admired her, and closely followed her son's slow change of heart. In 386 Augustine was converted, and at Easter 387 he was baptized. Soon afterward, while waiting for a ship to return to Africa, mother and son talked at a window in Ostia about eternal life, in a moment of deep peace that Augustine describes in the "Confessions." Monica said there was nothing left for her to desire in this world: she had seen her son a Christian.

"Remember me at the altar of the Lord"

A few days later she fell ill. She asked her sons to bury her anywhere and added: "I ask only that you remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you may be." She died in Ostia in 387, at about fifty-six years of age. Her relics are in Rome. She is the patron of mothers, of wives in difficult marriages and of all who pray perseveringly for the conversion of a loved one. Her feast is August 27, the day before the feast of Saint Augustine.
expedito:
A fourth-century martyr

Saint Expeditus appears in the Church's ancient martyrologies as a martyr of Melitene, in Lesser Armenia, a region of today's Turkey, killed on April 19 at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecution of Emperor Diocletian, together with other Christian companions. Historical information about his life is scarce, but the Church has always remembered him among those who gave their lives for Christ.

The Roman commander

According to tradition, Expeditus was the commander of a Roman legion, a man of prestige, used to military discipline and the honors of the Empire. At some point he came to know the Christian faith and felt God's call to leave the life he was living and follow Christ. He knew that, in a time of persecution, becoming a Christian could cost him his career and his very life.

"Today!"

A well-known legend tells that when he decided to convert, the devil appeared in the form of a crow crying "Cras! Cras!", which in Latin means "Tomorrow! Tomorrow!", trying to persuade him to put off his decision. Expeditus stepped on the crow and answered: "Hodie!", "Today!" That is why his images show him dressed as a Roman soldier, standing on a crow and holding a cross with the word "Hodie." The lesson is clear: do not leave until tomorrow the conversion and the good we can do today. Expeditus remained faithful unto martyrdom.

Patron of urgent causes

Because of this story and his very name, which suggests speed, Saint Expeditus became the patron of urgent causes and of those who need a quick solution. He is also invoked by students, soldiers and workers. In Brazil his devotion is very great, and on April 19 thousands of people visit his shrines to give thanks for graces received and to make their requests.
barbara:
The young woman in the tower

Saint Barbara is one of the most popular martyrs of the early Church, venerated from very early times in both East and West. She probably lived in the third century, and the details of her story have reached us through ancient accounts that mix fact and tradition. According to them, Barbara was the daughter of a rich pagan named Dioscorus, who, jealous of her beauty and wanting to keep suitors away, kept her shut up in a tower.

The three windows

In the solitude of the tower Barbara reflected on the meaning of life and came to know the Christian faith, probably through Christians who instructed her in secret, and she asked for Baptism. Tradition says that while her father was away she had a third window opened in a building of the house that was supposed to have only two, explaining later that the three windows represented the Holy Trinity, the light of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit that illuminated her soul.

Martyred by her own father

When he discovered that his daughter was a Christian and had refused marriage in order to consecrate herself to God, Dioscorus was furious and denounced her to the authorities. Barbara was tortured but remained firm in the faith. Condemned to death, according to tradition she was beheaded by her own father. Soon afterward, the account says, lightning struck Dioscorus and killed him.

Protector in storms

Because of this account, Saint Barbara came to be invoked against lightning, storms and sudden death, and she became the patron of artillerymen, miners, firefighters and all who work with explosives and fire. In Brazil many people pray to her when it thunders. Although little is known of her story with certainty, her memory remains alive as an example of courageous faith. Her feast is celebrated on December 4.
jose-anchieta:
From the Canaries to Coimbra

José de Anchieta was born on March 19, 1534, in San Cristóbal de La Laguna, on the island of Tenerife in the Canaries. He went to study in Coimbra, Portugal, where he excelled in literature and poetry. In 1551 he joined the Society of Jesus. Soon afterward he suffered a serious spinal injury that left him stooped for the rest of his life, and his superiors sent him to Brazil, hoping the climate would help him. He arrived in Bahia in 1553, only nineteen years old.

Founder of São Paulo

Together with Father Manuel da Nóbrega he climbed the coastal mountains and on January 25, 1554, took part in founding the college of São Paulo de Piratininga, in a simple hut, the origin of today's city of São Paulo. There he taught Latin to the young, catechized the indigenous people and cared for the sick. He learned Tupi so well that he wrote a grammar of the language, as well as catechisms, poems and plays to teach the faith in a joyful way, close to the local culture.

Hostage and poet

In 1563, during peace negotiations with the Tamoios, who were at war with the Portuguese, Anchieta stayed as a voluntary hostage at Iperoig, today Ubatuba. At risk of death, he composed a long Latin poem in honor of Our Lady, writing the verses in the sand on the beach and keeping them in his memory. Peace was achieved. Later he took part in the founding of Rio de Janeiro in 1565, was ordained a priest and, years later, governed all the Jesuits of Brazil as provincial.

The Apostle of Brazil

In old age he lived in Reritiba, in Espírito Santo, where he died on June 9, 1597. The indigenous people carried his body for dozens of kilometers to Vitória. He was beatified in 1980 by John Paul II and canonized by Pope Francis in 2014. He is called the Apostle of Brazil and is the patron of Brazilian catechists. His feast is June 9.
madre-paulina:
An immigrant girl

Amabile Lucia Visintainer was born on December 16, 1865, in Vigolo Vattaro, in Trentino, a region that now belongs to Italy. In 1875, at ten years old, she emigrated with her family to Brazil, where they settled in an immigrant colony called Vigolo, in Nova Trento, Santa Catarina. There Amabile helped at home, worked in the fields, taught catechism to the children, visited the sick and looked after the community chapel.

The hut at Vigolo

On July 12, 1890, together with her friend Virginia Nicolodi, she began caring for an abandoned woman sick with cancer in a small hut. That simple gesture gave rise to the Congregation of the Little Sisters of the Immaculate Conception, the first women's congregation founded in Brazil, approved by the bishop in 1895. Amabile received the name Sister Pauline of the Agonizing Heart of Jesus. The sisters lived poorly, working to support the sick, the elderly and children.

São Paulo and humiliation

In 1903 Mother Pauline moved to São Paulo, where the congregation began taking in orphans, children of people who had been enslaved and abandoned elderly people. She was elected superior general, but in 1909, because of disagreements and intrigues, she was removed from office by the archbishop and sent to work as an ordinary sister in Bragança Paulista, caring for the sick and the elderly. She accepted everything in silence and obedience, without complaint. Only many years later was she recognized and honored as foundress.

The first saint of Brazil

At the end of her life she suffered greatly from diabetes: she lost fingers, then an arm, and went blind, offering her pain to God. She died in São Paulo on July 9, 1942. She was beatified in Florianópolis in 1991 and canonized by Pope John Paul II on May 19, 2002, becoming the first saint who lived and carried out her work in Brazil. Her shrine in Nova Trento welcomes pilgrims from all over the country. Her feast is July 9.
edith-stein:
A Jewish philosopher seeking the truth

Edith Stein was born on October 12, 1891, in Breslau, then in Germany and today Wrocław in Poland, into an observant Jewish family. She was the youngest of eleven children, and her father died when she was two. As a teenager she stopped believing in God and stopped praying. Highly intelligent, she went to study philosophy in Göttingen with the famous Edmund Husserl, whose assistant she became. During the First World War she worked as a volunteer nurse in a military hospital.

"This is the truth"

The witness of Christian friends, especially the serenity of a widow facing her husband's death, began to touch her. In 1921, while staying at a friend's house, she took from the shelf the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Ávila and spent the whole night reading. When she finished, she said to herself: "This is the truth." On January 1, 1922, she was baptized in the Catholic Church. She began teaching at a school run by Dominican sisters and giving lectures throughout Germany, especially on the vocation and dignity of women.

A Carmelite in times of hatred

In 1933, when the Nazis came to power, she was forbidden to teach because of her Jewish origin. She wrote to Pope Pius XI asking the Church to speak out against the persecution of the Jews. That same year she entered the Carmel of Cologne, receiving the name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. To protect her, in 1938 she was transferred to the Carmel of Echt in the Netherlands, where her sister Rosa, also a convert, came to live with her. There she wrote "The Science of the Cross," on Saint John of the Cross.

Martyr at Auschwitz

In 1942, after the Dutch bishops publicly condemned the deportation of the Jews, the Nazis arrested Jews who had converted to Catholicism. On August 2 Edith and Rosa were taken; as they left she said to her sister: "Come, let us go for our people." She was killed in a gas chamber at Auschwitz on August 9, 1942. Canonized by John Paul II in 1998, she was proclaimed co-patroness of Europe in 1999. Her feast is August 9.
joao-bosco:
The dream at nine years old

John Bosco was born on August 16, 1815, in Becchi, a village in Piedmont in northern Italy, into a poor peasant family. His father died when he was two, and his mother, Margaret, raised him with faith and firmness. At nine he had a dream that marked his life: he saw boys fighting and cursing, and a man with a shining face told him that he would not win them over with blows but with gentleness and charity. The boys turned into wild beasts and then into little lambs.

The little acrobat

As a child he learned juggling and magic tricks to attract the village boys; after the show he repeated Sunday's sermon to them and prayed the Rosary. To be able to study he worked as a farmhand, tailor, blacksmith and waiter. He was ordained a priest in 1841 in Turin. Visiting the prisons, he was shocked to see so many young people imprisoned and abandoned, and he decided to devote his life to keeping others from ending up there.

The Oratory and the Salesians

On December 8, 1841, he began gathering street boys for catechism. After years without a fixed place, he settled in Valdocco, in Turin, where the Oratory of Saint Francis de Sales was born: home, school, workshop, playground and church all at once. His method, called the preventive system, was based on reason, religion and loving kindness: educating with joy, presence and trust. Among his students was Saint Dominic Savio. In 1859 he founded the Society of Saint Francis de Sales, the Salesians, and in 1872, with Saint Mary Dominic Mazzarello, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians. He built the basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin.

Father and teacher of youth

He died in Turin on January 31, 1888, telling his followers to love the young. He was canonized in 1934 and is called the "father and teacher of youth." The Salesians are present throughout the world today, including Brazil, whose future capital, Brasília, many link to one of his famous dreams. Don Bosco used to say: "It is enough that you are young for me to love you." His feast is January 31.
frei-galvao:
The boy from Guaratinguetá

Antônio Galvão de França was born in 1739 in Guaratinguetá, in the interior of São Paulo, into a wealthy, influential and very religious family. At thirteen he went to study with the Jesuits in Bahia. He thought of joining the Society of Jesus but, because of the persecution the Jesuits were beginning to suffer in Portugal, his father advised him to seek out the Franciscans. In 1760 he entered the Order of Saint Francis in Rio de Janeiro and was ordained a priest in 1762.

"Son and slave of Mary"

Sent to the Franciscan friary in São Paulo, he became a preacher, confessor and porter of the friary, receiving everyone who came to him with kindness. Deeply devoted to Our Lady, in 1766 he wrote and signed a document consecrating himself as "perpetual son and slave" of the Virgin Mary. People of every social class sought him out, considering him a man of God.

The Monastery of Light

He was confessor to a house of retreat for women, where he met Sister Helena Maria of the Holy Spirit, who said she had received from Jesus the request to found a new house of prayer. In 1774 Friar Galvão founded with her the Retreat of Our Lady of the Conception of Divine Providence, known today as the Monastery of Light (Mosteiro da Luz). He himself designed and oversaw the construction of the monastery and its church for almost thirty years, often carrying stones alongside the workers. The Monastery of Light is today a historic landmark of São Paulo.

Friar Galvão's pills

Once a young man suffering terrible pain from kidney stones came to him, and he wrote on a small slip of paper a Latin phrase in honor of Our Lady and asked him to swallow it with faith. The young man was healed. The same happened with a woman in a difficult childbirth. Thus were born "Friar Galvão's pills," which the sisters of the Monastery of Light still prepare today. Friar Galvão died on December 23, 1822, and is buried in the monastery. Canonized by Benedict XVI in São Paulo in 2007, he was the first saint born in Brazil.
teresinha:
The youngest of the Martin family

Thérèse Martin was born on January 2, 1873, in Alençon, France, the youngest of the five daughters of Louis and Zélie Martin, a very devout couple who were also canonized. At four she lost her mother to cancer, and the family moved to Lisieux. Extremely sensitive, she cried over anything. At ten she fell gravely ill and was healed, she said, by the smile of a statue of Our Lady. At Christmas 1886 she received the grace to overcome her excessive sensitivity, which she called her "conversion."

A Carmelite at fifteen

Two of her sisters had already entered the Carmel of Lisieux, and Thérèse wanted to follow them. Because she was so young, she went on pilgrimage to Rome and, against protocol, personally asked Pope Leo XIII for permission. On April 9, 1888, at fifteen, she entered the Carmel, receiving the name Thérèse of the Child Jesus and the Holy Face. There she lived a hidden life made of little things: smiling at an unpleasant sister, accepting a correction without excusing herself, working with love.

The little way

Thérèse discovered what she called the "little way": going to God with the trust and surrender of a child in its father's arms, offering every small gesture out of love. Reading Saint Paul, she understood that her vocation was love: "In the heart of the Church, my mother, I will be love." She prayed for missionaries and for the conversion of sinners. In 1896 she fell ill with tuberculosis and went through months of great physical suffering and a harsh trial of faith, without losing her trust.

A shower of roses

She died on September 30, 1897, at twenty-four, saying: "My God, I love you." Before dying she promised to spend her heaven doing good on earth and to let fall a "shower of roses." Her memoirs, published as "The Story of a Soul," spread throughout the world. She was canonized in 1925, proclaimed patroness of the missions in 1927 and a Doctor of the Church in 1997. Her feast is October 1.
clara-assis:
The young noblewoman who ran away from home

Clare was born around 1193 in Assisi, Italy, into a noble and wealthy family. From childhood she was known for her prayer and her charity toward the poor. Hearing the preaching of Francis of Assisi, she felt the desire to live as he did, poor and wholly given to God. On the night of Palm Sunday 1212, at eighteen, she ran away from home and went to the Portiuncula, where Francis and the friars were waiting for her. There he cut her hair and she received a simple habit.

The Poor Ladies of San Damiano

Her family tried to bring her back by force, but Clare clung to the altar and showed her shorn head, the sign of her consecration. Soon afterward her sister Agnes joined her, and later her mother and another sister as well. Francis settled them in the little church of San Damiano, which he himself had rebuilt. There the Order of Poor Ladies, the Poor Clares, was born, devoted to prayer, silence and poverty. Clare was abbess for more than forty years, serving her sisters with humility, washing their feet and caring for the sick.

The privilege of poverty

Clare firmly defended the right to live without property, trusting only in God's providence, and obtained from the popes the so-called "privilege of poverty." She was the first woman to write a rule of religious life for women that was approved by a pope, which happened two days before her death. Around 1240, when soldiers attacked the convent, Clare, though ill, had the Blessed Sacrament brought and prayed before it; the attackers fled. That is why she is depicted holding a monstrance.

Patroness of television

At Christmas 1252, very ill and unable to go to Mass, she said she saw and heard the celebration on the wall of her room. For that reason Pope Pius XII proclaimed her patroness of television. She died on August 11, 1253, and was canonized only two years later. Her name means "clear," luminous, and her life was a light for the whole Franciscan family. Her feast is August 11.
carlo-acutis:
An ordinary boy in love with the Eucharist

Carlo Acutis was born in London on May 3, 1991, to Italian parents who were working there, and a few months later the family returned to Milan. His parents were not very devout, but from an early age Carlo showed a special love for Jesus. He made his First Communion at seven, and from then on he tried to go to Mass every day and pray the Rosary. He said the Eucharist was his "highway to heaven." His faith ended up helping his family draw closer to God.

The computer kid

Carlo was a teenager like any other: he liked soccer, video games, making films with his pets and, above all, computers. He taught himself to program and build websites. He used this talent to evangelize: he put together an exhibition on the Eucharistic miracles recognized by the Church around the world, which was later shown in thousands of parishes on five continents. He limited his own time on games so as not to become their slave.

"Everyone is born an original"

At school he defended classmates who were bullied and helped those who were struggling. With his savings he bought sleeping bags and food for the homeless of Milan. He said that "everyone is born an original, but many die as photocopies," and that holiness means letting God act in us. In October 2006 he was diagnosed with a very aggressive leukemia. He offered his sufferings for the Pope and the Church and died a few days later, on October 12, only fifteen years old.

The first saint of the internet generation

His body rests in Assisi, the city he loved because of Saint Francis. He was beatified in 2020, after the healing of a boy in Campo Grande, Brazil, attributed to his intercession. On September 7, 2025, he was canonized by Pope Leo XIV together with Pier Giorgio Frassati. He is called the patron of the internet and is an example for young people of how to use technology for good. His feast is October 12.
chiara-luce:
The long-awaited daughter

Chiara Badano was born on October 29, 1971, in Sassello, a small town in Liguria, Italy, after her parents had waited and prayed for eleven years to have a child. She grew up joyful, generous and very sporty: she loved tennis, swimming, the mountains and being with her friends. At nine she met the Focolare Movement and began to live the Gospel in daily life with enthusiasm. The movement's foundress, Chiara Lubich, gave her the nickname "Luce," light, because of the joy she radiated.

"If you want it, Jesus, I want it too"

In 1988, at seventeen, she felt a sharp pain in her shoulder during a tennis match. Tests revealed a very aggressive bone cancer. After a first moment of silence and inner struggle, she gave everything to God with a phrase that became her motto: "If you want it, Jesus, I want it too." She underwent painful surgeries and treatments and lost the use of her legs, but she kept smiling. Whenever she could she refused morphine, so as to stay lucid and offer her pain out of love.

A light for others

Her hospital room, and later her home, became a place visited by many young people who came to console her and left consoled themselves. She paid attention to the other patients and gave her savings to a friend leaving on a mission to Africa. She prepared her own death like a wedding feast with Jesus: she chose a white dress, the music and the readings, and asked that no one cry but that everyone sing.

Blessed Chiara Luce

She died on October 7, 1990, at eighteen. Her last words were to her mother: "Goodbye, Mom, be happy, because I am." She was beatified in Rome on September 25, 2010, at a ceremony with thousands of young people. She is remembered as an example that it is possible to live holiness in youth, with joy, even in the midst of pain. Her memorial is celebrated on October 29.
pier-giorgio:
A rich young man from Turin

Pier Giorgio Frassati was born on April 6, 1901, in Turin, Italy, into a wealthy and influential family. His father, Alfredo, was the founder of the newspaper "La Stampa," a senator and later Italy's ambassador to Germany; his mother was a painter. His parents were not very religious, but Pier Giorgio developed a deep faith: he went to Mass and received Communion every day, prayed the Rosary and spent long hours in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament.

Friend of the poor

At seventeen he joined the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul and began visiting the poor and sick in the most wretched neighborhoods of Turin. He did it in secret, without his family knowing, giving away his money, his clothes and even his tram fare, then walking home. He studied mining engineering so that he could work alongside the miners, the most burdened of all workers. He took part in Catholic Action and political life, defending social justice and courageously opposing fascism. He was also a Dominican tertiary.

"To the heights"

Pier Giorgio was cheerful, playful and full of friends. He loved mountain climbing and went on long hikes with a group of friends who jokingly called themselves the "Shady Characters." On one of his most famous photos he wrote: "Verso l'alto," "To the heights," which became the motto of his life: always climbing, in the mountains and in holiness.

The man of the Beatitudes

In 1925, at twenty-four, he contracted a fulminant polio, probably caught from one of the sick people he visited. He died on July 4, after only a few days. At his funeral his family was amazed to see the streets filled with the poor he had quietly helped. John Paul II beatified him in 1990, calling him "the man of the eight Beatitudes," and Pope Leo XIV canonized him on September 7, 2025, together with Carlo Acutis. His feast is July 4.
domingos-savio:
"Death, but not sin"

Dominic Savio was born on April 2, 1842, in Riva, near Chieri in Piedmont, Italy, the son of a blacksmith and a seamstress who were very religious. From a young age he loved to pray and to serve at Mass. At seven, when First Communion was usually made later, he received permission to receive Communion and wrote some resolutions that guided his life, among them: "My friends will be Jesus and Mary" and "Death rather than sin."

Meeting Don Bosco

In 1854, at twelve, he met Saint John Bosco. During their conversation he said to him: "I am the cloth; you be the tailor. Make a beautiful garment of me for the Lord." Don Bosco welcomed him to the Oratory in Turin, where he lived with hundreds of poor boys. There Dominic understood that holiness did not lie in doing extraordinary penances but in carrying out each day's duties well, with joy. He told his companions: "Here we make holiness consist in being always cheerful."

An apostle among his classmates

Dominic was studious, a good friend and attentive to anyone who was sad or alone. Once, learning that two classmates were going to fight with stones, he stood between them holding a crucifix and asked that the first stone be thrown at him; the two gave up in shame. In 1856 he founded with some friends the Company of the Immaculate Conception, a group to pray, help their companions and look after newcomers to the Oratory.

Don Bosco's little saint

In fragile health, he developed a lung illness and was sent home to his parents. He died on March 9, 1857, only fourteen, saying with a radiant face: "What a beautiful thing I see!" Don Bosco wrote his biography, which inspired generations of young people. He was canonized in 1954 by Pope Pius XII, at the time the youngest saint who was not a martyr. He is the patron of altar servers and of expectant mothers. His feast is celebrated on May 6.
maria-goretti:
A poor family of farmworkers

Maria Goretti was born on October 16, 1890, in Corinaldo, Italy, into a very poor family of farmworkers. In search of work her parents moved to the marshlands near Nettuno, south of Rome, where they shared a house with another family, the Serenellis. In 1900 Maria's father died of malaria. Her mother, Assunta, had to work in the fields, and Maria, only nine years old, took over the housework and the care of her younger siblings. She was cheerful, obedient and very devout, and she made her First Communion with great joy.

"No! It is a sin!"

Alessandro Serenelli, a young man of twenty who lived in the same house, began to harass her. On July 5, 1902, taking advantage of their being alone, he tried to rape her. Maria resisted with all her strength, saying it was a sin and that God did not want it. Enraged, Alessandro stabbed her fourteen times and fled. Maria was taken to the hospital, where she suffered greatly for almost a whole day.

Forgiveness

Before she died, when the priest asked whether she forgave her attacker, Maria answered: "Yes, for the love of Jesus I forgive him, and I want him to be with me in Paradise." She received Communion and died on July 6, 1902, at eleven years old. Alessandro was sentenced to thirty years in prison. For years he showed no remorse, until he dreamed of Maria offering him lilies. From then on he was profoundly converted.

Saint of purity and forgiveness

On leaving prison, Alessandro went to ask forgiveness from Maria's mother, and the two received Communion together at Christmas Mass. He ended his life as a lay brother in a Capuchin friary. On June 24, 1950, Pope Pius XII canonized Maria Goretti before an immense crowd; among those present was her mother, the first mother to attend her daughter's canonization. Maria is the patron of youth and of purity. Her feast is July 6.
jose-sanchez-rio:
A boy in a time of persecution

José Sánchez del Río was born on March 28, 1913, in Sahuayo, in the state of Michoacán, Mexico. In the 1920s the government of President Plutarco Calles imposed extremely harsh laws against the Church: churches were closed, priests imprisoned and killed, and public worship forbidden. Many Catholics rose up to defend religious freedom in a conflict known as the Cristero War. Their cry was "Long live Christ the King!"

The little flag bearer

José's older brothers joined the Cristeros, and he, only thirteen, insisted on going too, saying it had never been so easy to win heaven. The commanders accepted him as a helper and flag bearer. In February 1928, during a battle, the general's horse was killed, and José gave him his own horse so he could escape. He stayed behind and was captured by government troops.

Faithful to the end

He was held in a church in Sahuayo that had been turned into a stable. They tried to persuade him to deny the faith in exchange for his freedom, even offering money and a comfortable life, but he refused. He wrote to his mother saying he was ready to die and asking her to accept God's will. On the night of February 10, 1928, they cut the soles of his feet and forced him to walk barefoot to the cemetery. At every step, when they ordered him to deny Christ, he cried out: "Long live Christ the King! Long live the Virgin of Guadalupe!" At the cemetery he was stabbed and shot to death. He was fourteen years old.

Martyr and saint

He was beatified in 2005 and canonized by Pope Francis on October 16, 2016. His story, also told in films, inspires young people around the world to live their faith with courage, even when it costs dearly. His feast is February 10.
kateri-tekakwitha:
The girl marked by smallpox

Kateri Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in Ossernenon, an indigenous village near today's state of New York, in the United States. Her father was a Mohawk chief and her mother a Christian Algonquin woman. At four, a smallpox epidemic killed her parents and her brother. She survived, but her face was scarred and her eyesight weakened. That is why she received the name Tekakwitha, often translated as "she who feels her way along." She was raised by an uncle, the village chief, who was opposed to the Christians.

Baptized at twenty

Kateri was shy, hardworking and very skilled at crafts. She refused the marriages arranged by her family, which caused great misunderstanding. When Jesuit missionaries passed through the village, she heard about Jesus and asked to be instructed. At Easter 1676, at twenty, she was baptized with the name Kateri, which means Catherine. Because of her faith she began to suffer mockery and threats, and some even wanted to kill her.

The mission of Kahnawake

In 1677 she fled, walking hundreds of kilometers, to a mission of Christian indigenous people called Kahnawake, near Montreal, Canada. There she could live her faith in peace. She went to Mass every day, spent long hours praying before the Blessed Sacrament, cared for the sick and the elderly and taught prayers to the children. In 1679 she made a vow of virginity, consecrating herself entirely to Christ, something unheard of among her people.

The Lily of the Mohawks

In fragile health, she died on April 17, 1680, only twenty-four years old. Her last words were: "Jesus, I love you." Witnesses said that soon after her death the smallpox scars disappeared from her face. She became known as the "Lily of the Mohawks." She was beatified in 1980 and canonized by Benedict XVI in 2012, the first indigenous saint of North America. She is the patron of ecology and of indigenous peoples. Her feast is July 14.
pastorinhos-fatima:
The cousins of Aljustrel

Francisco Marto was born on June 11, 1908, and his sister Jacinta on March 11, 1910, in Aljustrel, a small village in Fatima, Portugal. They were the children of a simple farming family and spent their days tending sheep with their older cousin, Lúcia dos Santos. Francisco was calm and contemplative; Jacinta, cheerful, lively and very sensitive. In 1916 the three received the visit of an angel, the Angel of Peace, who taught them to pray and to offer sacrifices to God.

The Lady brighter than the sun

On May 13, 1917, at the Cova da Iria, they saw a Lady dressed in white, "brighter than the sun," who asked them to return there on the thirteenth of each month until October. In the apparitions Our Lady asked them to pray the Rosary every day for peace in the world and for the conversion of sinners, and to offer sacrifices for them. In July she showed them a vision of hell and entrusted a secret to them. In August the children were detained and threatened by the local administrator, but they did not reveal the secret. On October 13, before some seventy thousand people, the so-called "miracle of the sun" took place.

Consoling Jesus and saving sinners

After the apparitions, Francisco spent hours in church before the tabernacle, saying he wanted to "console the hidden Jesus," who was sad because of sins. Jacinta, deeply affected by the vision of hell, offered many small sacrifices for the conversion of sinners and prayed a great deal for the Pope. In 1918 the Spanish flu struck both siblings.

The youngest saints

Francisco died at home on April 4, 1919, at ten years old. Jacinta suffered longer, underwent surgery and died alone in a Lisbon hospital on February 20, 1920, at nine, offering everything out of love. They were beatified by John Paul II in 2000 and canonized by Pope Francis in Fatima on May 13, 2017, the centenary of the apparitions, becoming the youngest non-martyr saints in the Church. Their feast is February 20.
laura-vicuna:
A Chilean girl in exile

Laura Vicuña was born on April 5, 1891, in Santiago, Chile. Her father, from an important family, lost everything in the country's political struggles and died when she was small. Left without means, her mother, Mercedes, fled with Laura and her younger sister to Argentina, in the Patagonia region. To survive, she went to live with a wealthy rancher named Manuel Mora, a violent man who kept her without marrying her and mistreated her.

The Salesian sisters' school

In 1900 Laura and her sister went to study at the boarding school of the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, the Salesian sisters, in Junín de los Andes. There Laura truly came to know the love of Jesus. She made her First Communion with great fervor and resolved to love God above all and to prefer death to offending him. She was cheerful, helpful and much loved by her classmates. She longed to become a religious sister, but suffered on realizing that her mother was living far from God.

The offering of her own life

During holidays at the ranch, Manuel Mora tried to abuse Laura, who firmly resisted. Deeply worried about her mother's salvation, Laura asked her confessor for permission to offer her own life to God for her mother's conversion. Soon afterward she fell gravely ill. In January 1904, when she refused to stay at the ranch, Mora beat her violently, worsening her condition.

Her mother's conversion

On her deathbed Laura told her mother what she had done: "Mama, I offered my life for you; I ask the Lord for your conversion." Moved, her mother promised to change her life. Laura died on January 22, 1904, at twelve years old, and her mother kept her promise, leaving Manuel Mora and returning to the sacraments. Laura was beatified by John Paul II in 1988. She is the patron of victims of abuse and of children who suffer in wounded families. Her memorial is celebrated on January 22.
solanus-casey:
The son of Irish immigrants

Bernard Francis Casey was born on November 25, 1870, on a farm in Wisconsin, in the United States, the sixth of sixteen children of an Irish immigrant couple. As a young man he worked as a lumberjack, a prison guard and a streetcar operator. One day, driving the streetcar, he saw a drunken man stab a woman in the street. Shaken, that night he felt a strong call to become a priest and to pray and work for the salvation of souls.

A "simplex" priest

In the seminary he had great difficulty with his studies, which were in German and Latin. In 1897 he entered the Capuchin friars in Detroit, receiving the name Solanus. Because of his poor exam results, he was ordained in 1904 as a "simplex priest": he could celebrate Mass but could not preach doctrinal sermons or hear confessions. He accepted this limitation with humility and without resentment.

The friary doorkeeper

He was appointed doorkeeper, first in friaries in New York and, from 1924, at Saint Bonaventure Monastery in Detroit. At the door he received dozens of people every day: the sick, the unemployed, families in crisis. He listened to each one patiently, prayed with them and invited them to trust in God. His most famous advice was: "Thank God ahead of time." Many healings and graces were attributed to his prayers. During the Great Depression that began in 1929, he helped found the Capuchin Soup Kitchen in Detroit, which still feeds the poor today.

Blessed Solanus

Even when he grew old and ill, he kept receiving those who came to him. He died in Detroit on July 31, 1957, saying: "I give my soul to Jesus Christ." Thousands of people came to his wake. He was beatified in Detroit in 2017 before a huge crowd. He is an example that God works powerfully through the humble. His memorial is celebrated on July 30.
miguel-pro:
A cheerful, playful young man

Miguel Agustín Pro was born on January 13, 1891, in Guadalupe, in the state of Zacatecas, Mexico. His father was a mining engineer, and Miguel grew up among the workers, who were very fond of him. He was full of humor and liked to imitate people, tell jokes and play the guitar. In 1911 he joined the Society of Jesus. Soon afterward, because of the Mexican revolution and the persecution of the Church, the novices had to flee the country.

Formed in exile

Miguel completed his studies in the United States, Spain, Nicaragua, where he taught, and Belgium, where he was ordained a priest in 1925. He suffered from a serious stomach ulcer and underwent several operations, but never lost his joy. In 1926 he returned to Mexico, just when President Calles had banned public worship, closed the churches and begun persecuting priests.

The priest in disguise

For more than a year Father Pro carried out his ministry underground in Mexico City. He wore disguises as a mechanic, a beggar, a businessman and even a police officer to move around the city. He celebrated Masses in homes, heard confessions, brought Communion to hundreds of people a day, baptized, married couples and helped poor families with food. He often narrowly escaped the police, always with good humor.

"Long live Christ the King!"

In November 1927, after an attack on a politician, Miguel and his brothers were arrested and accused without evidence. Without any trial he was sentenced to be shot. On November 23, 1927, before the firing squad, he forgave the soldiers, prayed, stretched out his arms in the shape of a cross, with his rosary in one hand, and cried out: "Long live Christ the King!" The government had the execution photographed to frighten Catholics, but the photos became a symbol of courage. He was beatified by John Paul II in 1988. His memorial is November 23.
basilio-magno:
A family of saints

Basil was born around 330 in Caesarea, in Cappadocia, in today's Turkey, into an extraordinary family: his grandmother Macrina, his parents Basil and Emmelia, his sister Macrina and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebaste are all venerated as saints. He studied at the best schools of Constantinople and Athens, where he formed a deep friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus, also a future saint. He came home a brilliant teacher and somewhat proud of his learning.

Monk and father of Eastern monasticism

It was his sister Macrina who helped him discover that true wisdom lay in following Christ. Basil asked for Baptism, visited the monks of Egypt, Syria and Palestine and then founded with friends a community of prayer and work in Pontus. He wrote rules for monastic life that valued community life, work and service to the poor. These rules are still followed today by many monks of the East.

Bishop of Caesarea

Ordained a priest, he was elected bishop of Caesarea in 370. He courageously defended the faith of the Council of Nicaea on the divinity of Christ against the Arians, who were supported by Emperor Valens. When a high official of the emperor threatened him and said no one had ever spoken to him so boldly, Basil replied: "Perhaps you have never met a bishop." During a great famine he organized food distribution and built on the outskirts of the city a large complex of charitable works, with a hospital, hostel and houses for the poor, which the people called the "Basiliad."

Doctor of the Church

He wrote an important treatise on the Holy Spirit, homilies and letters, and a liturgy still celebrated in the Eastern Churches is attributed to him. He died on January 1, 379, at about forty-nine. He is one of the great Fathers of the Church, a Doctor of the Church, called "the Great." His feast is celebrated on January 2, together with his friend Saint Gregory of Nazianzus.
isabel-ana-seton:
A young woman of New York society

Elizabeth Ann Bayley was born on August 28, 1774, in New York, into an Episcopalian family. Her mother died when she was three, and her father was a respected physician. In 1794 she married William Seton, a wealthy merchant, with whom she had five children. Although she moved in high society, she devoted herself to works of charity and helped found an association to assist poor widows with small children.

A widow in Italy

William's business failed and he fell ill with tuberculosis. In 1803 the couple traveled to Italy with their eldest daughter, hoping the climate would help him recover. On arrival they spent weeks in quarantine in a cold, damp place, and soon afterward William died. Elizabeth was welcomed by a family of Italian friends, the Filicchis, who took her to churches and explained the Catholic faith to her. She was deeply moved by faith in the real presence of Jesus in the Eucharist.

Conversion and its cost

Back in New York, after much reflection and prayer, she was received into the Catholic Church on March 14, 1805. Her conversion cost her dearly: relatives and friends turned away, and she struggled to support her children. In 1808 she was invited to open a school in Baltimore, and the following year in Emmitsburg, Maryland, she founded the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph, the first religious congregation of women founded in the United States.

Mother of American Catholic schools

With the sisters she opened a free school for poor girls, which became the beginning of Catholic parish schools in the United States. She suffered the loss of two daughters but kept her trust in God. She died of tuberculosis on January 4, 1821, at forty-six. She was canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1975, becoming the first saint born in the United States. Her feast is January 4.
andre-bessette:
An orphan in fragile health

Alfred Bessette was born on August 9, 1845, near Montreal, Canada, into a poor family. His father, a woodcutter, died in an accident when he was nine, and his mother died of tuberculosis three years later. Alfred was very frail and had almost no schooling: he could barely read and write. He worked on farms, as an apprentice in various trades and even in factories in the United States, always praying a great deal and with deep devotion to Saint Joseph.

"I am sending you a saint"

In 1870 he asked to enter the Congregation of Holy Cross. Because of his poor health he was nearly turned away, but his parish priest wrote to the superior: "I am sending you a saint." He received the name Brother André and was appointed doorkeeper of Notre-Dame College in Montreal. He himself would say with a smile: "When I joined the community, they showed me the door, and I stayed there forty years." Besides being doorkeeper, he was barber, messenger and cleaner.

Friend of Saint Joseph

At the door Brother André received students, parents and the sick. He prayed with them, encouraged them to trust in Saint Joseph and sometimes anointed them with oil from a lamp that burned before the saint's statue. Many people began saying they had been healed, and soon thousands of sick people were coming to see him. He always answered: "It is not I who heal, it is Saint Joseph." His great dream was to build a shrine in honor of Saint Joseph on Mount Royal. In 1904 he managed to build a small chapel with the coins he saved from cutting the students' hair.

Saint Joseph's Oratory

The little chapel grew into Saint Joseph's Oratory, the largest church in Canada, visited by millions of pilgrims. Brother André died on January 6, 1937, at ninety-one, and about a million people filed past his coffin. He was canonized by Benedict XVI in 2010. His memorial is celebrated on January 6.
raimundo-penafort:
The law professor of Barcelona

Raymond was born around 1175 at the castle of Penyafort, near Barcelona, in Catalonia. Very intelligent, he studied and taught law in Barcelona and later at the famous University of Bologna, in Italy, becoming a doctor of civil and canon law. He was known for teaching poor students free of charge. Returning to Barcelona, he became a canon of the cathedral and in 1222, already over forty, joined the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans.

Redeemer of captives

At that time many Christians were captured by pirates and sold as slaves. Raymond supported and helped Saint Peter Nolasco found the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, the Mercedarians, devoted to ransoming captives, whose members even offered themselves in exchange for prisoners. He also wrote a manual widely used by confessors to help them guide people with justice and mercy.

In the service of the Pope

In 1230 Pope Gregory IX called him to Rome as his confessor and gave him an enormous task: to organize all the laws of the Church, scattered across many different collections. Raymond gathered and ordered the documents in the so-called "Decretals," published in 1234, which served as the basis of Church law for almost seven hundred years. In 1238 he was elected master general of the Dominicans, but two years later he asked to resign and return to a life of prayer and preaching.

The saint who sailed on his cloak

In old age he encouraged the study of Arabic and Hebrew for dialogue with Muslims and Jews, and he asked Saint Thomas Aquinas to write a work to help missionaries. A well-known tradition says that when King James I of Aragon prevented him from leaving the island of Majorca, after Raymond had rebuked him for his immoral life, Raymond spread his cloak on the sea and sailed to Barcelona. He died almost a hundred years old on January 6, 1275. He was canonized in 1601 and is the patron of lawyers and students of law. His feast is January 7.
hilario-poitiers:
A pagan seeking the truth

Hilary was born around 315 in Poitiers, in Gaul, today's France, into a noble pagan family. He received an excellent education and, as an adult, married and the father of a daughter, began to search for the meaning of life and the truth about God. Dissatisfied with pagan philosophy, he found in the Scriptures, especially in the beginning of the Gospel of John, the answer he was looking for: God is one and has revealed himself in his Son, the Word made flesh. Around 345 he was baptized with his family.

Bishop and defender of the faith

Because of his exemplary life, the people chose him as bishop of Poitiers around 350. It was a time of great confusion in the Church because of Arianism, a heresy that denied that Jesus was truly God and that enjoyed the support of Emperor Constantius II. Hilary firmly defended the faith proclaimed at the Council of Nicaea. For this, in 356, he was condemned and exiled to Phrygia, in Asia Minor, far from his diocese.

A fruitful exile

The four years of exile were very fruitful. Hilary learned Greek, came to know the theology of the Eastern Fathers and wrote his principal work, "On the Trinity," which explains in depth the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For this courageous defense of the faith he was called "the Athanasius of the West." Returning to Poitiers in 360, he continued working for unity of faith in Gaul. He was also the friend and teacher of Saint Martin, who founded near Poitiers one of the first monasteries in the West.

Doctor of the Church

Hilary composed hymns in Latin so that the people could learn the faith by singing, and he was one of the first Christian hymn writers in the West. He died around 367 in Poitiers. In 1851 Pope Pius IX declared him a Doctor of the Church. His feast is celebrated on January 13.
antao-grande:
"Sell all that you have"

Anthony, also called Anthony the Abbot, was born around 251 in Egypt into a wealthy Christian family. At about twenty he lost his parents and became responsible for his younger sister. Soon afterward, entering a church, he heard the Gospel in which Jesus says to the rich young man: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." Anthony felt those words were meant for him. He sold his land, distributed the money to the poor, entrusted his sister to a community of consecrated women and began a life of prayer and penance.

In the desert

First he lived near his village, learning from older hermits, then in an old tomb and finally in an abandoned fort in the desert, where he stayed about twenty years. There he faced strong temptations and spiritual struggles, later depicted by many artists. He overcame them through prayer, fasting and trust in Christ. When he came out of solitude, many disciples wanted to live near him, and the desert filled with monks. That is why Anthony is called the father of monks.

Counselor and defender of the faith

Anthony left the desert only when the Church was in need: during a persecution he went to Alexandria to encourage the imprisoned Christians, and later he returned there to support Saint Athanasius against the Arians. People of every class, even emperors, wrote to him asking for advice. In old age he withdrew to a mountain near the Red Sea, where today there is a monastery bearing his name.

An example for all times

He died in 356 at about 105 years of age. Saint Athanasius wrote his biography, which spread quickly and inspired many people, among them Saint Augustine, who was deeply struck on hearing about it. Saint Anthony is the patron of domestic animals and of farmers, and on his feast, January 17, animals are blessed in many places.
ines-roma:
A courageous girl

Saint Agnes was a young Roman martyred at the beginning of the fourth century, probably during the persecution of Emperor Diocletian. Saint Ambrose, who wrote about her a few decades later, says she was only twelve or thirteen years old and marvels that so young a girl had a courage many adults lacked. From early on her tomb in Rome was greatly venerated, and her name was included in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

"Christ is my spouse"

According to tradition, Agnes came from a noble family and was very beautiful, and several important young men wanted to marry her, among them the son of a prefect of Rome. Agnes refused them all, explaining that she had already consecrated herself to Christ, whom she called her spouse. The rejected suitors denounced her as a Christian. Threatened with instruments of torture, she was not intimidated.

Martyrdom

The ancient accounts say that, to humiliate her, she was publicly exposed, but God protected her: her hair grew and covered her body, and a young man who tried to dishonor her fell as if dead, later revived by Agnes's own prayers. Condemned to be burned, the flames did not consume her. In the end she was killed by a sword stroke to the throat. Ambrose writes that she went to the place of execution more joyfully than a bride goes to her wedding.

The saint of the lamb

Agnes was buried on the Via Nomentana, where in the fourth century the daughter of Emperor Constantine had a basilica built in her honor. Her name recalls the Latin word "agnus," meaning lamb, which is why she is shown holding a lamb, a symbol of purity and of Christ, the Lamb of God. Every year on her feast, January 21, two lambs are blessed in Rome, and their wool is used to make the pallia the Pope gives to archbishops. She is the patron of girls and of purity.
conversao-paulo:
Saul, the zealous Pharisee

Saul was born in Tarsus, in Cilicia, today's Turkey, into a Jewish family that held Roman citizenship. He learned the trade of tentmaking and went to Jerusalem to study the Law with the great teacher Gamaliel. He became a Pharisee, very zealous for the traditions of his people. For this reason he saw the followers of Jesus as a threat. He was present at the stoning of Saint Stephen, guarding the cloaks of those who killed him, and then began to persecute the Christians, entering homes and dragging men and women off to prison.

On the road to Damascus

With letters from the high priest, he set out for Damascus to arrest the Christians of that city. On the way a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" He asked: "Who are you, Lord?" And the voice answered: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." Saul got up blind and was led by the hand into Damascus, where for three days he could not see, and neither ate nor drank, but prayed.

Ananias and baptism

The Lord appeared to a disciple named Ananias and sent him to find Saul. Ananias was afraid, for he knew the persecutor's reputation, but Jesus told him: "This man is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles." Ananias laid his hands on Saul, and something like scales fell from his eyes. He regained his sight, was baptized and at once began to proclaim in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. His former allies now wanted to kill him, and the Christians helped him escape from Damascus by lowering him over the wall in a basket.

The Apostle to the Gentiles

Saul, who came to be known by his Roman name Paul, became the great missionary to the pagan world. He made long journeys through Asia Minor, Greece and Italy, founded communities and wrote letters that are part of the New Testament. He was imprisoned, flogged and shipwrecked, yet he said: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me." He died a martyr in Rome. The Church celebrates his conversion on January 25, the day that closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.
angela-merici:
A girl from Lake Garda

Angela Merici was born on March 21, 1474, in Desenzano, on the shores of Lake Garda in northern Italy. She grew up in a deeply Christian farming family, where the lives of the saints were read aloud in the evenings. While still a teenager she lost her parents and went to live with an uncle in Salò. She also suffered greatly from the sudden death of her older sister and prayed for her salvation. She joined the Third Order of Saint Francis, living with great simplicity, prayer and penance.

The vision of the ladder

According to tradition, one day while praying in the fields Angela had a vision: a ladder rising to heaven, on which young women were climbing, accompanied by angels. She understood that God was calling her to gather young women consecrated to him. She also saw that many girls grew up with no religious instruction at all, and she began to teach the catechism to the children of her area. In 1516 she moved to Brescia, where she became known as a counselor to both simple people and nobles.

Pilgrim and faithful to her mission

In 1524 she made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. During the journey she went blind, but she chose to continue and visited the holy places with faith, unable to see. On the way back she regained her sight while praying before a crucifix at the same place where she had lost it. The following year in Rome, Pope Clement VII invited her to stay and work in the city, but she understood that her mission was in Brescia.

The Company of Saint Ursula

On November 25, 1535, Angela founded the Company of Saint Ursula with twenty-eight young women. It was something new: the women consecrated themselves to God but continued living in their own homes, serving their families and the Church and teaching the faith to girls. Angela told her daughters: "Do something, get moving, be confident; the Lord will help." She died in Brescia on January 27, 1540. The work grew and gave rise to the Ursulines, who are devoted to education throughout the world. She was canonized in 1807. Her memorial is celebrated on January 27.
sao-bras:
Physician and bishop in Armenia

Saint Blaise lived between the third and fourth centuries and was bishop of Sebaste, in ancient Armenia, a city now called Sivas, in Turkey. What we know of his life has come to us mainly through ancient accounts written some time after his death. According to this tradition, before becoming bishop he was a physician who cared not only for the bodies but also for the souls of the sick. Because of his goodness and holiness, the people chose him as their shepherd.

The bishop of the cave

When persecution of Christians began under Emperor Licinius, Blaise took refuge in a cave on the mountain, from which he continued to guide the faithful. It is said that wild animals came to him, and he blessed them and healed those that were wounded. One day hunters looking for beasts for the circus games found the cave surrounded by animals, with the bishop praying in their midst. They took him prisoner to the governor.

The choking boy

On the way to prison a desperate mother brought him her son, who was dying, choking on a fish bone stuck in his throat. Blaise laid his hands on the boy, prayed and blessed him, and the child was healed. Tradition also tells that a poor woman whose only pig had been carried off by a wolf got the animal back through the saint's prayer. Later she visited Blaise in prison, bringing food and candles to light his dark cell.

Martyrdom and the blessing of throats

Because he refused to worship the pagan gods, Blaise was tortured with iron combs used for carding wool and finally beheaded, around the year 316. Because of the boy's healing, he is invoked against ailments of the throat. On his feast, February 3, in many churches priests bless the throats of the faithful with two crossed candles, recalling the candles the woman brought to the prison, and pray: "Through the intercession of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat and from every other illness."
santa-agueda:
A consecrated young woman of Sicily

Saint Agatha lived in Sicily, in southern Italy, in the third century and was martyred in Catania around the year 251, during the persecution of Emperor Decius. Her cult is very ancient, and her name was included in the Roman Canon of the Mass, together with other virgin martyrs. The accounts of her martyrdom, written later, say that she came from a noble family, was very beautiful and had consecrated her life and her virginity to God from her youth.

Refusing the governor

The governor of Sicily, named Quintianus, wanted to take her as his wife. When Agatha refused him, he used the law against Christians to pressure her. First he handed her over for a month to a woman of bad life, hoping she would abandon her faith and her purity. But Agatha stood firm, praying: "Jesus Christ, Lord of all things, you see my heart and know my desire: possess all that I am." Before the tribunal she calmly declared that being a servant of Christ was true nobility.

The tortures and the visit of Saint Peter

Furious, Quintianus had her cruelly tortured and even ordered her breasts to be cut off. Thrown into prison without care, Agatha was visited during the night, according to tradition, by the apostle Saint Peter, who healed her wounds. After this she was dragged over burning coals. At that moment an earthquake shook the city, and the frightened people demanded that it stop. Agatha was taken back to prison, where she died praying on February 5, 251.

Protector of Catania

A year after her death, Mount Etna erupted, and the lava advanced toward Catania. The inhabitants carried in procession the veil that covered the saint's tomb, and the lava stopped. Since then Agatha has been venerated as a protector against fire and eruptions, and her feast is one of the greatest in Sicily. She is also the patron of nurses and of women suffering from diseases of the breast. Her memorial is celebrated on February 5.
paulo-miki:
The faith reaches Japan

In 1549 Saint Francis Xavier brought the Gospel to Japan, and within a few decades the faith had spread: there were hundreds of thousands of Japanese Christians. Paul Miki was born around 1564 near Kyoto, the son of a military leader who became a Christian. He was baptized as a child and educated at the Jesuit seminary, where he stood out for his intelligence and faith. He joined the Society of Jesus and became a highly esteemed preacher, because he knew the religions of Japan well and knew how to speak to the hearts of his people.

The persecution

The ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who at first tolerated Christians, grew suspicious of them and in 1587 ordered the expulsion of the missionaries. In 1596, after a Spanish ship was wrecked on the coast of Japan and rumors spread that the missionaries were preparing a foreign conquest, he had Christians arrested. Twenty-six were seized: six foreign Franciscan friars, among them the Mexican Saint Philip of Jesus; three Japanese Jesuits, among them Paul Miki, who was close to being ordained a priest; and seventeen Japanese lay people, including catechists and three boys.

The long march

The prisoners had part of their left ear cut off and were forced to walk in winter for about a month from Kyoto to Nagasaki, passing through towns to serve as an example. Along the way they prayed, sang and encouraged the Christians they met. The boy Louis Ibaraki, twelve years old, refused an offer to be freed if he renounced the faith.

On the hill of Nagasaki

On February 5, 1597, they were crucified on a hill in Nagasaki and killed with lances. From the cross Paul Miki preached for the last time: he said he was dying for proclaiming the Gospel and declared that he forgave the ruler and all who were responsible for his death, asking that they too might receive Baptism. The twenty-six martyrs were canonized in 1862. The faith they watered with their blood survived in hiding in Japan for more than two hundred years. Their memorial is February 6.
josefina-bakhita:
A kidnapped girl

Bakhita was born around 1869 in a village in the Darfur region of Sudan. She lived happily with her family until, at about seven or eight years old, she was kidnapped by slave traders. The fear and suffering were so great that she forgot her own name. Her kidnappers began calling her Bakhita, which in Arabic means "fortunate." She was sold several times in the slave markets and suffered terrible abuse. One of her owners had dozens of cuts made on her body as a tattoo, leaving her scarred for life.

On the way to freedom

In 1883 in Khartoum she was bought by the Italian consul Callisto Legnani, who treated her kindly. Two years later he took her to Italy, where she stayed with the Michieli family as nanny to the couple's daughter. When Mrs. Michieli had to travel, she left Bakhita and the girl with the Canossian Sisters in Venice. There Bakhita came to know God. She said that since childhood, looking at the sky, she had wondered who could have made so many beautiful things. Now she discovered his name: God, who loved her.

"I am free"

When Mrs. Michieli returned to take her away, Bakhita calmly refused to go. The case went to court, and on November 29, 1889, it was decided that in Italy she was free. On January 9, 1890, she received Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion, taking the name Josephine. In 1896 she became a Canossian sister.

The "Brown Mother"

She lived more than forty years in Schio, in northern Italy, as cook, sacristan and doorkeeper. She was so kind and cheerful that the people affectionately called her the "Brown Mother." She said that if she met those who had kidnapped her, she would kneel and kiss their hands, because if that had not happened, she would not have come to know Jesus. She died on February 8, 1947, and was canonized by John Paul II in 2000. She is the patron of Sudan and of victims of human trafficking. Her memorial is February 8.
cirilo-metodio:
Two brothers from Thessalonica

Methodius and Constantine, who later took the name Cyril, were brothers born in Thessalonica, Greece, in the ninth century: Methodius around 815 and Constantine around 827. Their father was an official of the Byzantine Empire, and many Slavic peoples lived in the region, so the boys grew up knowing their language. Constantine studied in Constantinople and excelled so much that he was called "the Philosopher." Methodius came to govern a province and later became a monk.

The mission to Moravia

In 862 Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia, a region that today is part of the Czech Republic and Slovakia, asked the emperor in Constantinople for missionaries who would teach the faith to his people in their own language. The two brothers were sent. For this, Constantine created an alphabet to write the Slavic language, called Glagolitic, and the brothers translated the Gospels and the texts of the liturgy. For the first time the Slavs could hear the Word of God and pray the Mass in their own tongue.

Approval in Rome

Some clergy of Germanic origin opposed them, saying the liturgy could only be celebrated in Hebrew, Greek or Latin. So the brothers went to Rome, where Pope Adrian II received them with honor and approved the Slavic books, placing them on the altar of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major. In Rome Constantine fell ill, became a monk with the name Cyril and died on February 14, 869. He was buried in the Basilica of San Clemente.

Patrons of Europe

Methodius was ordained a bishop and returned to the mission. His opponents even imprisoned him for more than two years until the Pope intervened to free him. He continued translating the Bible until his death on April 6, 885. His disciples carried the work to Bulgaria, where the Cyrillic alphabet arose, named in honor of Cyril and still used in several countries today. In 1980 John Paul II proclaimed the two brothers patrons of Europe. Their feast is celebrated on February 14.
pedro-damiao:
A poor boy from Ravenna

Peter was born in 1007 in Ravenna, Italy, the youngest of a large, poor family. He was orphaned very young and went to live with an older brother who treated him badly and set him to tending pigs. Another brother, named Damian, who was a priest, took pity on him, brought him home and paid for his studies. In gratitude Peter also took his brother's name, which is why he became known as Peter Damian. He studied in Faenza and Parma and became a famous teacher.

The hermit of Fonte Avellana

Despite his success, Peter felt that God was calling him to something greater. Around 1035 he entered the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, in the Apennine mountains, where the monks lived in small cells in silence, prayer, fasting and work. Soon afterward he became prior of the community, which grew greatly under his direction. He wrote about the life of prayer, composed hymns and prayers and encouraged devotion to Our Lady.

Reformer of the Church

At that time the Church suffered from serious problems: church offices were bought with money, and many clergy lived unworthy lives. Peter Damian, with strong words and the example of his own poor life, fought for priests and bishops to return to living according to the Gospel. The Popes began to seek his advice, and in 1057, against his will, he was named cardinal and bishop of Ostia. He carried out several important missions to settle conflicts and correct abuses in different regions.

Back to solitude

Peter asked many times to give up his offices and return to the hermit's life, and at last he obtained permission. Even so, he still accepted some missions when the Pope needed him. Returning from one of them, in Ravenna, he fell ill and died in Faenza on February 22, 1072. In 1828 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. His memorial is celebrated on February 21.
policarpo:
Disciple of the apostle John

Polycarp was born around the year 69 and was bishop of Smyrna, a city in Asia Minor now called Izmir, in Turkey. Saint Irenaeus, who knew him as a boy, relates that Polycarp had lived with the apostle Saint John and with others who had seen the Lord, and that he loved to repeat what he had heard from them about Jesus. For this reason Polycarp is a bridge between the apostles and the following generations of Christians.

Shepherd and friend of saints

Around the year 107, Saint Ignatius of Antioch, being taken as a prisoner to be martyred in Rome, passed through Smyrna, was welcomed by Polycarp and later wrote him a letter full of affection and advice. From Polycarp's own hand we have a letter to the Christians of Philippi, in which he urges them to faith, charity and fidelity. In old age he went to Rome to speak with Pope Anicetus about the date of Easter, which was celebrated on different days in the East and the West. They did not reach agreement, but they parted in peace, and the Pope invited him to celebrate the Eucharist.

"Eighty-six years I have served him"

Around the year 155, during a persecution, the crowd in Smyrna demanded Polycarp's arrest. He took refuge on a farm, but when the soldiers arrived he had food served to them and asked only for time to pray. In the stadium the proconsul urged him to curse Christ and save his life. Polycarp replied: "Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never done me any wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?"

The martyrdom

Condemned to be burned, he prayed, thanking God for counting him among the martyrs. According to the account of witnesses, the flames formed something like a ship's sail around his body without burning it, and then an executioner killed him with a dagger. The Christians gathered his bones, "more precious than precious stones," and began to celebrate the day of his martyrdom every year. This account is one of the oldest about a Christian martyr. His memorial is celebrated on February 23.
cassimiro:
A prince of Poland

Casimir was born on October 3, 1458, in Kraków, Poland. He was the son of King Casimir IV, who ruled Poland and Lithuania, and of Queen Elizabeth of Austria, and the second son of a large family. His teacher was the priest and historian Jan Długosz, who educated the princes with discipline and a deep Christian formation. From his youth Casimir stood out for his prayer, purity of life and simplicity, even though he lived in a court full of luxury.

The Hungarian campaign

In 1471, when he was only thirteen, a group of Hungarian nobles dissatisfied with their king offered Casimir the crown of Hungary. His father sent him at the head of an army to take the throne. The expedition failed: the nobles who had invited him were reconciled with their king, and the unpaid soldiers began to desert. Casimir returned home. It is said that from this experience he understood better how fleeting the glories of this world are.

A just regent and friend of the poor

Between 1481 and 1483, while his father was in Lithuania, Casimir governed Poland as regent and showed great wisdom, justice and care for the weakest. He visited the poor and the sick and shared what he had with them. He spent long hours praying before the Blessed Sacrament, sometimes at night at the doors of closed churches. He had a great devotion to Our Lady and loved to pray a Marian hymn that he asked to have placed with him in his tomb. He declined a proposed marriage to the emperor's daughter, wishing to remain celibate.

Patron of Lithuania

Ill with tuberculosis, he died on March 4, 1484, in Grodno, at only twenty-five, and was buried in the cathedral of Vilnius, in Lithuania, where his body is venerated in a beautiful chapel. He was canonized in the sixteenth century. He is the patron of Lithuania, of Poland and of young people. His memorial is celebrated on March 4.
perpetua-felicidade:
Two young women of Carthage

In the year 203, in Carthage, North Africa, Emperor Septimius Severus had forbidden anyone to become a Christian. Even so, a group of catechumens, people preparing for Baptism, remained firm in the faith. Among them were Vibia Perpetua, a noble young woman of twenty-two, married and the mother of a baby she was still nursing, and Felicity, a slave who was eight months pregnant. With them were arrested Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus, and later their catechist, Saturus, who gave himself up voluntarily to be with them.

Perpetua's diary

In prison Perpetua wrote a diary that has come down to us and is one of the oldest writings by a Christian woman. She tells how her father, who was not a Christian, came several times to beg her to renounce the faith. Pointing to a jug, she asked him whether it could be called anything other than what it was. Her father said no. "So I too cannot be called anything other than what I am: a Christian." She was baptized while in custody and had visions in which she climbed a ladder to heaven, stepping on the head of a dragon that guarded its foot.

Felicity's courage

Felicity feared that, being pregnant, she might not be able to die with her companions, for the law forbade executing pregnant women. They all prayed, and two days before the games she gave birth to a girl, who was adopted by a Christian woman. When she groaned in labor, a guard mocked her, saying she would suffer far more before the beasts. She answered: "Now it is I who suffer; there, another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I will suffer for him."

In the amphitheater

On March 7, 203, the martyrs were led into the amphitheater. Perpetua entered singing. The two young women were thrown before a wild cow and were wounded.
