Perpetua lifted Felicity from the ground, and the two exchanged the kiss of peace before being killed by the sword. Their names are in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Their memorial is celebrated on March 7.
joao-de-deus:
A boy who left home

John Cidade was born on March 8, 1495, in Montemor-o-Novo, Portugal. At eight years old, for reasons no one fully knows, he left home and ended up in Oropesa, Spain, where he grew up working as a shepherd for a farmer. As a young man he enlisted as a soldier and fought in the wars of Emperor Charles V, leading a dissolute life. Later he was a shepherd again, worked in North Africa helping an impoverished Portuguese family and finally became a seller of books and religious images in Granada, Spain.

The "madman" of Granada

Around 1537, when he was over forty, he heard a sermon by Saint John of Ávila and was so moved that he began crying out for God's mercy, tore up the books he sold, gave away everything he had and walked the streets weeping for his sins. The people thought he was mad, and he was confined in the royal hospital, where the mentally ill were treated with whippings. Saint John of Ávila visited him and helped him turn that fervor into service to those who suffered as he did.

"Do good, brothers"

In 1539 John rented a house in Granada and began taking in the poor sick, the abandoned and the homeless. At night he went through the streets with a basket on his back, begging alms and saying: "Do good to yourselves, brothers!" He himself washed, fed and cared for each patient, treating them with dignity. A bishop gave him the name by which he became known: John of God. During a fire at the royal hospital he went into the burning building several times and brought the patients out without being burned.

Patron of hospitals

In 1550, trying to save a young man drowning in the Genil River, he fell gravely ill. He died on March 8 of that year, his birthday, kneeling before a crucifix. His companions continued the work and formed the Hospitaller Order of Saint John of God, which today cares for the sick in dozens of countries. He was canonized in 1690 and is the patron of hospitals, the sick and nurses. His memorial is March 8.
francisca-romana:
A noble girl who wanted to be a nun

Frances was born in 1384 in Rome, into a noble and wealthy family. From childhood she prayed a great deal and wished to become a religious sister. But, as was the custom of the time, her parents arranged her marriage when she was only twelve, to Lorenzo Ponziani, a young Roman nobleman. Frances obeyed and was a devoted wife. The marriage, which lasted about forty years, was happy, and the couple had three children.

Wife, mother and servant of the poor

Together with her sister-in-law Vannozza, who became her great friend, Frances visited the hospitals and the poor of Rome, bringing food and clothing and caring for the sick. She is said to have taught that a married woman must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her household tasks. She lived through very hard times: Rome was invaded, the family palace was looted, her husband was wounded and her eldest son was even taken hostage. During an epidemic of plague and a great famine she lost two of her children, yet she turned her own home into a hospital and gave everything she had to those in need.

The guardian angel

Frances had a very deep life of prayer and received mystical graces. According to the accounts of her confessor, for many years she saw her guardian angel at her side, guiding her and, at night, lighting the way when she went out to help someone. For this reason, in 1925 Pope Pius XI declared her patron of motorists.

The Oblates of Tor de' Specchi

In 1425 Frances gathered a group of Roman women who wanted to serve God and the poor without leaving their families, and who later came to live in community: the Oblates of Mary, linked to the Olivetan Benedictine monks. After her husband's death in 1436, Frances went to live with them and became their superior. She died on March 9, 1440, and was canonized in 1608. She is the patron of Rome, of homemakers and of widows. Her memorial is March 9.
sao-patricio:
A slave in Ireland

Patrick was born around the year 385 in Roman Britain. His father was a deacon and a town official, and his grandfather a priest, but Patrick himself tells us that in his youth he did not take the faith seriously. At sixteen he was captured by Irish raiders and taken as a slave to Ireland, where he spent six years tending flocks in the mountains, suffering hunger and cold. It was there, in solitude, that he discovered God: he would pray a hundred times during the day and as many at night.

Escape and calling

One day he heard in a dream a voice saying that a ship was ready to take him home. He fled, walked many miles to the coast and managed to get on board. Back with his family, he had another dream: a man handed him letters headed "The voice of the Irish," and he heard the people of Ireland pleading: "We beg you, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more." Patrick understood that God was calling him to return as a missionary to the land where he had been a slave. He prepared, studied and was ordained a priest.

Apostle of Ireland

Around 432, now a bishop, he returned to Ireland. For about thirty years he traveled the island, preaching, baptizing thousands, ordaining priests and founding churches and communities. He faced the opposition of pagan chiefs and priests, was imprisoned several times and was in danger of death. Tradition says he used the shamrock, a small three-leafed plant, to explain the mystery of the Holy Trinity. He wrote the "Confession," in which he humbly recounts his life, and a courageous letter against a chieftain who had killed and enslaved newly baptized Christians.

"Christ with me"

A beautiful prayer known as "Saint Patrick's Breastplate" is attributed to him, which says: "Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me." He died on March 17, around the year 461. He is the patron of Ireland, and his day, March 17, is celebrated by Irish people all over the world.
cirilo-jerusalem:
Catechist of the Holy City

Cyril was born around the year 315 in or near Jerusalem, a few years after Emperor Constantine granted freedom to Christians. He received a good formation in the Scriptures and was ordained a priest. The bishop entrusted him with a very important task: preparing the catechumens, the adults who would receive Baptism on Easter night. Around the year 348, in the great Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the place of Jesus' death and resurrection, Cyril preached a series of catecheses that were written down and have come down to us.

The Catecheses

In these sermons Cyril explains the Creed phrase by phrase, simply and profoundly, and after Baptism he explains to the newly baptized the meaning of the sacraments they had received. He speaks with great faith of Christ's presence in the Eucharist and teaches how to receive it with reverence: "When you approach, make your left hand a throne for your right, which is to receive the King." These catecheses are still a treasure for understanding how the first Christians lived the faith and the liturgy.

Bishop and three times exiled

Around 350 Cyril became bishop of Jerusalem. Soon after, in 351, a great luminous cross appeared in the sky over the city, and he wrote to the emperor reporting the event. His time as bishop was marked by many struggles: a neighboring bishop who favored the Arians accused him unjustly, even of having sold church objects, when in fact he had sold them to feed the poor during a famine. Cyril was driven from his diocese three times, spending about sixteen years in exile.

Doctor of the Church

In 378 he was able to return to Jerusalem for good, and in 381 he took part in the Council of Constantinople, which confirmed the faith of Nicaea and completed the Creed we still pray today. He died in 386. In 1883 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church. His memorial is celebrated on March 18.
turibio-mogrovejo:
A Spanish jurist

Turibius Alfonso de Mogrovejo was born on November 16, 1538, in Mayorga, Spain. He studied law at the universities of Valladolid, Salamanca and Coimbra, in Portugal, and became a professor. He was known for his intelligence, uprightness and life of prayer. King Philip II appointed him judge of an important tribunal in Granada, a post he held with justice, although he was a layman with no plans to become a priest.

From layman to archbishop

In 1579, to everyone's surprise, the king nominated him to be archbishop of Lima, Peru, a huge and difficult diocese in the New World. Turibius protested that he was not even a priest, but in the end he accepted it as God's will. He received holy orders, was ordained a priest and then a bishop in 1580, and arrived in Lima in 1581. His diocese stretched over thousands of kilometers of deserts, Andean mountains and forests.

The shepherd who crossed the Andes

Turibius learned Quechua and other indigenous languages so he could preach to and hear the confessions of the people directly. He visited the entire diocese three times, often on foot or by mule, facing cold, hunger and danger, over a total of thousands of kilometers. According to the accounts, he confirmed hundreds of thousands of people, among them Saint Rose of Lima. He firmly defended the indigenous people against the abuses of the Spanish colonizers, including powerful officials, which made him many enemies.

Organizer of the Church in America

In 1582 he convened the Third Council of Lima, which prepared a catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, one of the first books printed in South America. In 1591 he founded in Lima one of the first seminaries on the continent, as well as churches and hospitals. He died during a pastoral visit, in Saña, on Holy Thursday, March 23, 1606. He was canonized in 1726 and is the patron of the bishops of Latin America. His memorial is celebrated on March 23.
francisco-paula:
A child asked of Saint Francis

Francis was born on March 27, 1416, in Paola, in Calabria, southern Italy. His devout parents went for years without being able to have children and asked Saint Francis of Assisi for the grace, promising to give the boy the saint's name. When their son was born, they kept the promise. At thirteen Francis spent a year in a Franciscan friary, where he impressed the friars with his prayer and obedience. Afterward he made a pilgrimage with his parents to Assisi and Rome.

The hermit who founded the Minims

At fifteen he decided to live as a hermit in a cave near Paola, devoted to prayer and penance. Soon other young men wished to live as he did, and so a new religious community was born, which later received the name Order of Minims, meaning "the least of all," because of its humility. Besides the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, the Minims took a vow to live always as in Lent, eating no meat, eggs or dairy. Francis's motto was a single word: "Charity."

Wonder-worker and friend of the poor

Many miracles were attributed to his prayers, and both the poor and the rich sought him out. It is said that in 1464, when a boatman refused to take him free of charge across the Strait of Messina, between Italy and Sicily, Francis spread his cloak on the water and crossed the sea with his companions. For this he is the patron of seafarers. He defended the poor before the powerful and was not afraid to correct unjust kings and nobles.

Counselor of kings

In 1483 King Louis XI of France, gravely ill, asked the Pope to send Francis to heal him. He went out of obedience to the Pope. He did not heal the king, but he helped him prepare to die at peace with God. He remained in France for twenty-five years, advising the following kings and founding friaries. He died on Good Friday, April 2, 1507, at ninety-one, and was canonized in 1519. His memorial is celebrated on April 2.
isidoro-sevilha:
A family of saints

Isidore was born around the year 560, probably in Cartagena, Spain, into a noble family that later moved to Seville. Three of his siblings are also venerated as saints: Leander and Fulgentius, who were bishops, and Florentina, who was an abbess. Since his parents died early, Isidore was educated by his older brother Leander, bishop of Seville, who was very demanding in his studies. A tradition says that, discouraged, the boy ran away from home, but on seeing how drops of water had worn a hole in a stone beside a well, he understood that perseverance overcomes all things and went back to his studies.

Bishop of Seville

At that time Spain was ruled by the Visigoths, who followed Arianism, a heresy that denied the divinity of Christ. Leander helped bring about the conversion of King Reccared and his people to the Catholic faith in 589. Around the year 600 Isidore succeeded his brother as bishop of Seville and governed the diocese for about thirty-six years. He presided over important councils, such as the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which called for schools for the formation of clergy beside the cathedrals. He also cared for the liturgy proper to Spain at that time.

The man who wanted to preserve all knowledge

Isidore was the most learned man of his time. His most famous work, the "Etymologies," is a great encyclopedia in twenty books that gathers the knowledge of the age: theology, grammar, history, medicine, geography, natural sciences and much more. Throughout the Middle Ages it was one of the most copied and studied books in Europe. He also wrote a history of the Goths and various works on the Bible and Christian life.

Doctor of the Church

Old and ill, he asked public forgiveness for his faults, distributed his goods to the poor and died in Seville on April 4, 636. In 1722 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. Because he gathered and organized so much knowledge, many remember him as a possible patron of the internet, although this is not official. His memorial is celebrated on April 4.
vicente-ferrer:
A Dominican from Valencia

Vincent Ferrer was born on January 23, 1350, in Valencia, Spain. At seventeen he entered the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. He studied philosophy and theology in Barcelona, Lleida and Toulouse and soon became a well-known teacher and preacher. He was a man of intense prayer, fasting and great charity, and the example of his life made his words even more powerful.

Amid the Great Schism

Vincent lived in one of the saddest periods in the history of the Church, the Great Western Schism, when there were at the same time two and later even three men claiming to be Pope, one in Rome and another in Avignon, France. Christians were divided, and even holy people supported different sides. Vincent, in good faith, supported the Avignon Pope, Pedro de Luna, whose confessor he was. In 1398, gravely ill, he had a vision of Christ accompanied by Saint Dominic and Saint Francis, sending him to preach conversion throughout the world. He was healed and set out.

The preacher of Europe

For twenty years Vincent traveled on foot and by donkey through Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland, preaching in the open air to immense crowds, sometimes of thousands. He spoke of God's love, of repentance and of the Last Judgment, and many sinners were converted, enemies were reconciled and whole towns changed their ways. Many miracles were attributed to him. It is said that he preached in his own language, Valencian, and yet people of other languages understood him.

Working for unity

In time Vincent realized that Pedro de Luna refused to resign in order to end the division. In 1416 he withdrew his support, and this did much to end the schism, with the election of a single Pope, Martin V, in 1417. Vincent died in Vannes, in Brittany, France, on April 5, 1419. He was canonized in 1455. His memorial is celebrated on April 5.
joao-batista-lasalle:
A wealthy young man from Reims

John Baptist de La Salle was born on April 30, 1651, in Reims, France, the eldest child of a wealthy noble family. He felt the call to the priesthood very early, and at sixteen he was already a canon of Reims cathedral, a prestigious position. He studied in Paris, but when he was about twenty his parents died and he had to return home to care for his younger siblings. Even so, he continued his studies, was ordained a priest in 1678 and earned a doctorate in theology.

Meeting the poor schoolmasters

In 1679 he met Adrien Nyel, a layman who wanted to open free schools for the poor boys of Reims. John Baptist began to help him, without imagining where it would lead. Seeing that the teachers were poorly trained and discouraged, he took them to live in his own house to form them, which scandalized his family and society. Little by little he understood that God was calling him to devote his whole life to the education of the poor. In 1683 he gave up his canonry and, during a great famine, distributed his entire fortune to those in need.

The Brothers of the Christian Schools

With the teachers he founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools, religious laymen entirely devoted to teaching. Their schools brought many innovations: pupils were taught in classes rather than one by one; lessons were in French rather than Latin; teaching was free for the poor. He also created schools to train teachers, Sunday schools for young workers and technical courses. He faced lawsuits, the opposition of schoolmasters who felt threatened and even misunderstanding within the Church, but he never gave up.

Patron of teachers

He died on Good Friday, April 7, 1719, in Rouen, saying: "I adore in all things the will of God in my regard." He was canonized in 1900, and in 1950 Pope Pius XII declared him patron of teachers. Today Lasallian schools are found in dozens of countries. His memorial is celebrated on April 7.
